edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Quaesisti proxime, Fabi frater, fugiendum necne sit in persecutione, quod nescio quid annuntiaretur. Ibidem ego oblocutus aliquid pro loco ac tempore, et quarumdam personarum importunitate, semitractatam materiam abstuli mecum, plenius eam de stylo nunc renuntiaturus, utpote quam mihi et tua consultatio commendarat, et conditio temporum suo jam nomine injunxerat. Quanto enim frequentiores imminent persecutiones, tanto examinatio procuranda est, quomodo eas excipere fides debeat. Procuranda autem examinatio penes vos, qui, si forte, Paracletum non recipiendo deductorem omnis veritatis, merito adhuc etiam aliis quaestionibus obnoxii estis. Igitur consultationi tuae ordinem quoque induimus, animadvertentes ante determinari oportere de statu ipsius persecutionis, utrum a Deo obveniat, an a diabolo, quo facilius de obitu ejus constare possit. Omnis enim rei inspectio, auctore cognito, planior. Satis est quidem praescribere nihil fieri sine Dei voluntate. Sed non statim hac sententia caeteris retractatibus locum dabimus, ne a praesenti articulo avocemur, si quis responderit: Ergo et malum a Deo, et delictum a Deo; nihil jam in diabolo, nihil etiam in nobis ipsis. De persecutione nunc quaeritur. Circa hanc interim dixerim nihil fieri sine Dei voluntate, respiciens eam in primis dignam Deo esse, et, ut ita dixerim, necessariam, ad probationem scilicet servorum ejus sive reprobationem. Quis est enim exitus persecutionis, quis effectus alius, nisi probatio et reprobatio fidei, qua suos utique Dominus examinavit? Hoc omne judicium est persecutio per quam quis aut probatus aut reprobatus judicatur. Porro judicium soli Deo competit. Haec pala illa, quae et nunc Dominicam aream purgat, Ecclesiam scilicet, confusum acervum fidelium eventilans, frumentum martyrum et paleas negatorum. Haec enim, scalae quas somniat Jacob, aliis ascensum in superiora, aliis descensum ad inferiora demonstrantes. Sic et agonem intelligi capit persecutionem. A quo certamen edicitur, nisi a quo corona et praemia proponuntur? Legis edictum agonis istius in Apocalypsi, quibus praemiis ad victoriam invitet, vel maxime illos qui proprie vicerint in persecutione, vincendo luctati, revera non adversus carnem et sanguinem, sed adversus spiritalia nequitiae. Ita agnosces ad eumdem agonothetam pertinere certaminis arbitrium, qui invitat ad praemium. Totum quod agitur in persecutione, gloria Dei est probantis et reprobantis, imponentis et deponentis. Quod autem ad gloriam Dei pertinet, utique ex voluntate illius eveniet. Sed quando Deus magis creditur, nisi cum magis timetur, nisi in tempore persecutionis? Tunc Ecclesia in attonito est; tunc et fides in expeditione sollicitior et disciplinatior in jejuniis et stationibus, et orationibus, et humilitate, in alterutra diligentia et dilectione, in sanctitate et sobrietate. Non enim vacatur nisi timori et spei. Adeo et ex hoc ipso ostenditur nobis non posse diabolo deputari eam, quae meliores efficit Dei servos. Si quod iniquitas a Deo non est, sed a diabolo, persecutio autem ex iniquitate consistit (quid enim iniquius quam veri Dei antistites, omnis sectatores veritatis, nocentissimorum more tractari?), ideo videtur persecutio a diabolo evenire, a quo iniquitas agitur, ex qua constat persecutio: seire debemus, quatenus nec persecutio est sine iniquitate diaboli, nec probatio fidei sine persecutione, propter probationem fidei necessariam iniquitatem, non patrocinium praestare persecutioni, sed ministerium; praecedere enim Dei voluntatem circa fidei probationem, quae est ratio persecutionis, sequi autem diaboli iniquitatem ad instrumentum persecutionis, quae ratio est probationis. Nam et alias, in quantum justitiae iniquitas aemula est, in tantum materia est ad testimonia ejus, cujus est aemula; ut sic justitia in iniquitate perficiatur, quomodo virtus in infirmitate perficitur. Nam infirma mundi electa sunt a Deo, ut confundantur fortia; et stulta ejus, ut confundantur sapientia. Ita et iniquitas adhibetur ut justitia probetur, confundens iniquitatem. Igitur quod ministerium non est arbitrii, sed servitii (arbitrium enim Domini, persecutio, propter fidei probationem, ministerium autem iniquitas diaboli, propter persecutionis instructionem); ita eam per diabolum, si forte, non a diabolo evenire credimus. Nihil Satanae in servos Dei vivi licebit, nisi permiserit Dominus, ut aut ipsum destruat per fidem electorum in tentatione victricem: aut homines ejus fuisse traducat, qui defecerint ad illum. Habes exemplum Job, cui diabolus nullam potuit incutere tentationem, nisi a Deo accepisset potestatem, nec in substantiam quidem ejus, nisi Dominus, Ecce, dixisset, omnia quae sunt ei, in manu tua do, in ipsum autem ne extenderis manum. Denique nec extendit, nisi posteaquam et hoc postulanti Dominus, Ecce, dixisset, trado tibi illum, tantum animam ejus custodi. Sic et in Apostolos facultatem tentationis postulavit, non habens eam nisi ex permissu. Siquidem Dominus in Evangelio ad Petrum: Ecce, inquit, postulavit Satanas uti cerneret vos velut frumentum: verum ego rogavi pro te, ne deficeret fides tua: id est, ne tantum diabolo permitteretur, ut fides periclitaretur. Quo ostenditur, utrumque apud Deum esse, et concussionem fidei, et protectionem, cum utrumque ab eo petitur, concussio a diabolo, protectio a Filio. Et utique cum Filius Dei protectionem fidei habet in sua potestate quam a Patre postulat, a quo omnem accipit potestatem in coelis et in terris, quale est ut concussionem fidei diabolus in manu sua habeat? Sed in legitima Oratione cum dicimus ad Patrem: Ne nos inducas in tentationem (quae aut major tentatio quam persecutio?); ab eo illam profitemur accidere, a quo veniam ejus deprecamur: hoc est enim quod sequitur: Sed erue nos a maligno; id est, ne nos induxeris in tentationem, permittendo nos maligno. Tunc enim eruimur diaboli manibus, cum illi non tradimur in tentationem. Nec in porcorum gregem diaboli legio habuit potestatem, nisi eam de Deo impetrasset, tantum abest ut in oves Dei habeat. Possum dicere, porcorum quoque setas tunc numeratas apud Deum fuisse; nedum capillos sanctorum. Habere videtur diabolus propriam jam potestatem, si forte in eos qui ad Deum non pertinent, semel in stillam situtae, et in pulverem areae, et in salivam nationibus deputatis a Deo, ac per hoc diabolo expositis in vacuam quodammodo possessionem. Caeterum, in domesticos Dei nihil illi licet ex propria potestate; quia quando liceat, id est, ex quibus caussis, exempla in Scripturis signata demonstrant. Aut enim ex caussa probationis conceditur ei jus tentationis provocato vel provocanti, ut in superioribus: aut ex caussa reprobationis traditur ei peccator quasi carnifici in poenam, ut Saul: Et abscessit, inquit, spiritus Domini a Saule, et concutiebat eum spiritus nequam a Domino, et suffocabat. Aut ex caussa cohibitionis, ut Apostolus refert datum sibi sudem angelum Satanae ut colaphizetur: nec hanc speciem permitti diabolo in sanctos humiliandos per carnis vexationem, nisi simul ut et virtus tolerantiae scilicet in infirmitate perfici possit; nam et ipse Apostolus Phigellum et Hermogenem tradidit Satanae, uti emendentur, ne blasphement. Vides jam et a servis Dei facilius diabolum accipere potestatem, tanto abest ut eam ex proprietate possideat. Cum ergo et haec exempla magis in persecutionibus eveniant, siquidem magis tunc probamur vel reprobamur, et magis tunc humiliamur vel emendamur, ab eo permittatur vel imperetur necesse est catholice fieri haec, a quo et ex parte, scilicet ab illo qui dicit: Ego sum qui facio pacem, et condo mala, id est bellum. Hoc est enim contrarium paci. Nostrae autem paci quid est bellum, quam persecutio? Si persecutionis vel maxime exitus aut vitam afferunt aut mortem, aut plagam aut sanationem, habes auctorem ejusdem: Ego percutiam, et sanabo; ego vivificabo, et mortificabo. Uram, inquit, illos, sicut uritur argentum; et probabo, inpuid, illos, sicut probatur aurum. Cum enim exurimur persecutionis ardore, tunc probamur de fidei tenore. Haec erunt ignea jacula diaboli, per quae fidei ustio et conflatio administratur; ex Dei tamen voluntate. De isto quis dubitare possit ignoro, nisi plane frivola et frigida fides, deprehendens eos qui timide conveniunt in Ecclesiam. Dicitis enim, Quoniam incondite convenimus, simul convenimus, et complures concurrimus in Ecclesiam, quaerimur a nationibus, et timemus ne turbentur nationes. Annon scitis quod Deus omnium sit Dominus? Et si velit Deus, tunc persecutionem patieris; si vero noluerit, silebunt nationes. Credas utique; si tamen in eum Deum credis, sine cujus voluntate nec passer unius assis cadit in terram. Nos autem, puto, multis passeribus antistamus. Igitur si constat a quo persecutio eveniat, possumus jam consultationem tuam inducere, et determinare ex hoc ipso praetractatu, fugiendum in persecutione non esse. Si enim persecutio a Deo evenit, nullo modo fugiendum erit quod a Deo evenit. Sicut duplex ratio defendit, quia neque debeat devitari, neque evadi possit quod a Deo evenit. Non debet devitari, quia bonum. Necesse est enim bonum esse omne quod Deo visum est. Et numquid ideo in Genesi sic positum est: Et vidit Deus quia bonum est; non quod ignoraret bonum esse, nisi vidisset; sed ut hoc sono portenderet bonum esse, quod Deo visum est? Multa quidem sunt, quae a Deo eveniant, et alicujus malo eveniant. Imo bonum est ideo, quia a Deo evenit, ut divinum et rationale. Quid enim divinum non rationale, non bonum? Quid bonum non divinum? Si autem sensui cujusque videtur, non sensus hominis praejudicat statui, sed status sensui. Status enim uniuscujusque certum quid est, et dat sensui legem, ita sentiendi statum, sicuti est. Si autem statu quidem bonum quod a Deo venit (nihil enim a Deo non bonum, quia divinum, quia rationale), sensui vero malum videtur, erit status in tuto, sensus in vitio. Statu optima res pudicitia, et veritas, et justitia, quae a multorum sensu displicent. Nunquid ideo status sensui addicitur? Ita et persecutio statu bona est, quia divina et rationalis dispositio;
pass_a_gloss: You have recently asked, brother Fabius, whether one should flee in persecution, because something was being announced, I do not know what. There, I, having spoken something on the spot and at the time, and because of the importunity of certain persons, took away with me the half-treated matter, now about to fully relate it from my writing, as your consultation and the condition of the times have commended it to me. For as much as persecutions are more frequent, so much must the examination be sought, how faith ought to receive them. But the examination must be sought by you, who, if perhaps you have not received the Paraclete, the guide of all truth, are still liable to other questions. Therefore, I am introducing order to your consultation, noticing that it must first be determined about the state of persecution itself, whether it comes from God or from the devil, so that it may be more easily agreed upon about its occurrence. For every inspection of a thing is clearer when the author is known. It is enough to prescribe that nothing happens without God's will. But we will not immediately give place to this opinion, lest we be called away from the present article, if someone responds: Therefore, evil is also from God, and sin is from God; nothing is now in the devil, nothing even in ourselves. Now, it is being asked about persecution. Concerning this, I will say in the meantime that nothing happens without God's will, looking at it as being especially worthy of God and, so to speak, necessary, for the testing of His servants or their rejection. For what is the outcome of persecution, what other effect, except the testing and rejection of faith, by which the Lord has certainly examined His own? This whole judgment is persecution, through which someone is judged either approved or rejected. Furthermore, judgment belongs to God alone. This is the fan that even now purifies the Lord's threshing floor, the Church, winnowing the confused heap of the faithful, the wheat of martyrs and the chaff of deniers. For this is the ladder that Jacob dreamed of, showing to some the ascent to higher things, to others the descent to lower things. Thus, persecution can also be understood as a contest. By whom is the contest announced, except by Him who offers the crown and rewards? The edict of this contest is in the Apocalypse, with what rewards it invites to victory, especially those who have properly conquered in persecution, having struggled and overcome, truly not against flesh and blood, but against spiritual wickedness. So, you will recognize that the judgment of the contest belongs to the same judge who invites to the reward. Everything that is done in persecution is for the glory of God, who tests and rejects, who imposes and deposes. But what pertains to the glory of God certainly happens by His will. But when is God more believed, except when He is more feared, except in the time of persecution? Then the Church is in astonishment; then faith is more solicitous and disciplined in fasts and stations, and prayers, and humility, in diligence and love, in sanctity and sobriety. For nothing is done except in fear and hope. So much so that it is also shown from this that it cannot be attributed to the devil, that which makes God's servants better. If some wickedness is not from God, but from the devil, and persecution consists of wickedness (for what is more wicked than that the priests of the true God, all followers of truth, are treated like the most wicked?), therefore, it seems that persecution happens by the devil, by whom wickedness is done, from which persecution consists: we ought to know that persecution is not without the devil's wickedness, nor is the testing of faith without persecution, because of the necessary wickedness for the testing of faith, not to patronize persecution, but to minister to it; for the will of God precedes concerning the testing of faith, which is the reason for persecution, but the devil's wickedness follows as an instrument of persecution, which is the reason for testing. For also, inasmuch as wickedness is a rival of justice, it is material for the testimonies of the one whose rival it is, so that justice may be perfected in wickedness, just as virtue is perfected in weakness. For the weak things of the world have been chosen by God to confound the strong, and the foolish things, to confound the wise. So also, wickedness is used to prove justice, confounding wickedness. Therefore, what is not a ministry of judgment, but of service (for the judgment is the Lord's, persecution, for the testing of faith, a ministry, but the devil's wickedness, for the instruction of persecution); thus, we believe that it happens through the devil, if perhaps, not by the devil. Nothing will be permitted to Satan against the living servants of God, except what the Lord permits, so that either He may destroy him through the victorious faith of the elect in temptation, or He may hand over those who have defected to him. You have the example of Job, to whom the devil was not able to bring any temptation, except what he had received from God, nor even against his substance, except after the Lord had said, 'Behold, everything that he has is in your hand, do not stretch out your hand against him.' Finally, he did not stretch out his hand, except after the Lord had said to him who was asking, 'Behold, I give him to you, only keep his soul.' So also, he asked for the power of temptation against the Apostles, not having it except by permission. Indeed, the Lord in the Gospel to Peter: 'Behold, Satan has asked to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail,' that is, that it may not be permitted to the devil to the extent that faith is endangered. By which it is shown that both the shaking of faith and its protection are with God, since both are asked from Him, the shaking from the devil, the protection from the Son. And certainly, when the Son of God has the protection of faith in His power, which He asks from the Father, from whom He receives all power in heaven and on earth, what kind of thing is it that the devil has the shaking of faith in his hand? But in the legitimate Prayer, when we say to the Father: 'Do not lead us into temptation' (what greater temptation than persecution?); we profess that it happens from Him, from whom we beg for its forgiveness: for this is what follows: 'But deliver us from evil,' that is, do not lead us into temptation, permitting us to the evil one. For then we are delivered from the devil's hands, when we are not handed over to him in temptation. Nor did the legion of demons have power over the herd of swine, except what they had obtained from God, so much less do they have power over the sheep of God. I can say that even the bristles of the swine were numbered by God at that time; how much more the hairs of the saints? The devil seems to have his own power, if perhaps in those who do not belong to God, once they have been given over to him, and to the dust of the threshing floor, and to the saliva of the nations, appointed by God, and thus exposed to the devil in a kind of empty possession. Nevertheless, in the household of God, nothing is permitted to him from his own power; for when it is permitted, that is, from what causes, the examples marked in the Scriptures demonstrate. For either the right of temptation is granted to him because of the cause of testing, provoked or provoking, as in the preceding examples; or because of the cause of rejection, the sinner is handed over to him as to an executioner for punishment, as with Saul: 'And the spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him, and suffocated him.' Or because of the cause of restraint, as the Apostle reports that a thorn in the flesh was given to him, an angel of Satan to buffet him; nor is this kind of thing permitted to the devil in the saints, to humble them through the vexation of the flesh, except that the virtue of endurance may also be perfected in weakness; for the Apostle himself handed over Philetus and Hermogenes to Satan, that they might be corrected, lest they blaspheme. You see now that the devil more easily receives power from the servants of God, so much less does he possess it from his own property. When, therefore, these examples happen more in persecutions, since we are more tested or rejected then, and more humbled or corrected then, it is necessary that these things be permitted or commanded by God, from whom both the testing and the protection are asked. For our peace, what is war, except persecution? If the outcomes of persecution bring either life or death, either plague or healing, you have the author of it: 'I will strike, and I will heal; I will kill, and I will make alive.' 'I will refine them,' He says, 'like silver; and I will test them, like gold.' For when we are refined by the fire of persecution, then we are tested by the tenor of faith. These will be the fiery darts of the devil, by which the burning and testing of faith are administered; however, from God's will. Who can doubt about this, except one with a frivolous and cold faith, seizing those who timidly come together in the Church? For you say: 'Since we come together in disorder, and many of us come together in the Church, we are sought by the nations, and we fear lest the nations be disturbed.' Do you not know that God is the Lord of all? And if God wills, then you will suffer persecution; if, however, He does not will, the nations will be silent. You ought to believe; if, indeed, you believe in that God, without whose will not even a sparrow falls to the ground. But we, I think, are worth many sparrows. Therefore, if it is agreed from whom persecution comes, we can now introduce your consultation, and determine from this very preface that one should not flee in persecution. For if persecution comes from God, it will not be fled from in any way, because it comes from God. As the double reason defends, because neither should it be avoided, nor can it be evaded, what comes from God. It should not be avoided, because it is good. For it is necessary that everything that has been seen by God is good. And is it not thus written in Genesis: 'And God saw that it was good'; not because He did not know it was good, unless He had seen; but that He might portend by this sound that it is good, what has been seen by God? Many things, indeed, happen from God, and happen for some evil. Nay, it is good, because it happens from God, as divine and rational. For what is divine not rational, not good? What is good not divine? If, however, it seems to someone's sense, not the sense of man prejudges the state, but the state prejudges the sense. For the state of each thing is a certain thing, and it gives the sense a law, so to sense the state, as it is. But if, indeed, the state is good, what comes from God (for nothing from God is not good, because it is divine, because it is rational), but to the sense it seems evil, the state will be in safety, the sense in vice. The state is optimal in chastity, and truth, and justice, which are displeasing to the sense of many. Should the state, therefore, be subject to the sense? So also, persecution is good by state, because it is a divine and rational disposition;

pass_b_english: You asked recently, brother Fabius, whether we ought to flee when persecution breaks out, prompted by some rumor I haven't quite caught. I did speak on the spot, but the pressure of certain people forced me to walk away with the matter only half-treated. Now I'm setting it down in full, as your request and the times themselves demanded. The more frequent the persecutions, the more urgently we need to work out how faith should receive them. That work falls to you — and it's a fair question whether you're up to it, since you've refused the Paraclete, the guide into all truth (John 16:13), leaving you still liable to every other doubt. So I'll impose some order on your inquiry. First, we must decide the nature of persecution itself: does it come from God or the devil? The answer makes it far easier to settle what happens in it. Any investigation clears up once the author is known. It's a baseline that nothing happens without God's will. But I won't let that axiom swallow the whole argument right away, or someone will retort: 'Then evil comes from God, sin comes from God; the devil has nothing left, and neither do we.' The question at hand is persecution. For now, I say it happens by God's will — looking at it as something peculiarly worthy of God, even necessary, for the testing or the rejection of his servants. What else is the outcome of persecution but the testing and rejection of faith, by which the Lord has always examined his own? (John 15:20; 1 Peter 4:12) Persecution is the whole judgment: through it a person is judged either approved or rejected. And judgment belongs to God alone. It's the winnowing fan that even now cleanses the Lord's threshing floor — the Church — tossing the mixed heap of the faithful, separating the wheat of martyrs from the chaff of deniers. (Matthew 3:12) It's the ladder Jacob dreamed of, showing some the ascent to higher things, others the descent to lower. (Genesis 28:12) You can read persecution as a contest, too. Who announces the contest but the one who offers the crown and the rewards? The edict of this contest stands in the Apocalypse, listing the prizes that call us to victory — above all for those who have truly conquered in persecution, struggling and winning not against flesh and blood but against spiritual wickedness. (Revelation 2:10; Ephesians 6:12) So you'll see the judging of the contest belongs to the same judge who invites to the reward. Everything done in persecution serves the glory of God, who tests and rejects, who raises up and casts down. And whatever serves God's glory certainly happens by his will. When is God more believed than when he is more feared — if not in the time of persecution? Then the Church stands in awe; then faith grows more earnest and disciplined in fasts, vigils, prayers, humility, in diligence and love, in holiness and self-control. Nothing is done except in fear and hope. That alone shows it can't be the devil's work — what makes God's servants better. If wickedness is not from God but from the devil, and persecution consists of wickedness — for what is more wicked than treating the priests of the true God, all followers of truth, like the vilest criminals? — then persecution seems to come from the devil, from whom wickedness proceeds and by which persecution consists. But we must grasp this: persecution is not without the devil's wickedness, nor is the testing of faith without persecution. The necessary wickedness serves the testing of faith — not as a patronage of persecution, but as its ministry. God's will precedes, aimed at the testing of faith, which is the reason for persecution; the devil's wickedness follows as the instrument of persecution, which is the reason for the testing. Wickedness rivals justice, and in that rivalry it becomes the material for the testimony of the one it rivals, so that justice is perfected in wickedness, just as virtue is perfected in weakness. (2 Corinthians 12:9) God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong, the foolish to shame the wise. (1 Corinthians 1:27) So wickedness is employed to prove justice, confounding wickedness itself. This ministry is not one of judgment but of service — judgment is the Lord's, persecution for the testing of faith; the ministry is the devil's wickedness, for the arrangement of persecution. Thus we believe it happens *through* the devil, not *by* the devil. Nothing is permitted to Satan against the living servants of God except what the Lord allows — either to destroy him through the victorious faith of the elect in temptation, or to hand over those who have defected to him. You have the case of Job: the devil could inflict no temptation until he received power from God, nor even touch his substance until the Lord said, 'Behold, all he has is in your hand; only do not stretch out your hand against him.' (Job 1:12) And he did not stretch it out until the Lord granted even that: 'Behold, I give him to you; only spare his life.' (Job 2:6) The same with the Apostles: he asked for the power to tempt them, and had it only by permission. The Lord told Peter in the Gospel: 'Behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail' (Luke 22:31-32) — that is, it would not be permitted to the devil to the point of endangering faith. This shows both the shaking of faith and its protection are with God, since both are asked of him: the shaking from the devil, the protection from the Son. And when the Son of God holds the protection of faith in his power, asked from the Father from whom he receives all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18), how could the devil hold the shaking of faith in his own hand? In the Lord's Prayer, when we say to the Father, 'Lead us not into temptation' — what greater temptation than persecution? — we confess it comes from him from whom we beg deliverance: 'But deliver us from evil' (Matthew 6:13), that is, do not lead us into temptation by handing us over to the evil one. We are snatched from the devil's hands precisely when we are not handed over to him in temptation. The legion of demons had no power over the herd of swine except what they obtained from God (Mark 5:12-13); how much less over the sheep of God? I'll say even the bristles of the swine were numbered by God then; how much more the hairs of the saints? (Luke 12:7) The devil appears to have his own power only over those who do not belong to God — once given over to him, like a drop in a bucket, dust on the threshing floor, spittle of the nations appointed by God and thus exposed to the devil in a kind of empty possession. (Isaiah 40:15) But in God's household, nothing is permitted to him from his own authority. Scripture's examples show when and why permission is granted: either the right of temptation is granted for the sake of testing, whether provoked or provoking, as in the cases above; or for the sake of rejection, the sinner is handed over to him as executioner for punishment, as with Saul: 'The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and a harmful spirit from the Lord tormented him' (1 Samuel 16:14); or for the sake of restraint, as the Apostle recounts — a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to buffet him (2 Corinthians 12:7) — not permitted in the saints to humble them through fleshly vexation except so that the virtue of endurance may be perfected in weakness; for the Apostle himself handed Hymenaeus and Alexander over to Satan, that they might learn not to blaspheme. (1 Timothy 1:20) You see now that the devil receives power more readily *from* the servants of God — so far from possessing it by right. Since these examples occur most in persecutions, when we are more tested or rejected, more humbled or corrected, they must be permitted or commanded by God — from whom both the testing and the protection are sought. For our peace, what is war but persecution? If persecution's outcomes bring either life or death, wound or healing, you have its author: 'I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal' (Deuteronomy 32:39). 'I will refine them like silver, and test them like gold' (Zechariah 13:9). When we are refined by persecution's fire, then we are tested by the tenor of faith. These are the devil's fiery darts (Ephesians 6:16), by which the burning and testing of faith are administered — yet from God's will. Who could doubt this except a frivolous, cold faith that seizes on those who timidly gather in the Church? You say: 'We meet in disorder, we crowd together, many of us, and the nations take notice; we fear they'll be disturbed.' Do you not know God is Lord of all? If God wills, you will suffer persecution; if he does not, the nations will be silent. You ought to believe — if you believe in that God without whose will not a single sparrow falls to the ground. (Matthew 10:29) And we, I think, are worth many sparrows. So, once it's settled where persecution comes from, we can bring your inquiry to a conclusion: from this very preamble it follows that one must not flee in persecution. If persecution comes from God, there is no fleeing what comes from God. A double reason defends this: what comes from God must not be avoided, and cannot be evaded. It must not be avoided because it is good. Everything God has seen fit to do is necessarily good. Isn't that why Genesis says: 'And God saw that it was good' (Genesis 1:10) — not because he didn't know it was good unless he looked, but to signal by this very phrasing that whatever God has seen is good? Many things happen from God and turn out evil for someone. Yet they are good *because* they come from God — as divine and rational. What is divine is not irrational, not evil. What is good is not undivine. If it seems evil to someone's sense, it is not human sense that judges the state of things, but the state that judges the sense. The state of a thing is fixed, and it gives sense its law: to perceive the state as it is. If the state is good — what comes from God (for nothing from God is not good, because it is divine, because it is rational) — but sense perceives it as evil, the state remains secure, the sense is in error. Chastity, truth, justice are optimal by state, yet displeasing to many people's sense. Should the state therefore be subjected to sense? So too persecution is good by state, because it is a divine and rational disposition.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological distinctions of Tertullian regarding the agency of God and the devil in persecution. All scripture citations in Pass B (e.g., John 16:13, Job 1:12, Matthew 6:13, etc.) correctly identify the underlying Latin allusions or direct quotes. The distinction between 'through' the devil (per diabolum) and 'by' the devil (a diabolo) is preserved. The translation of 'status' as 'state' in the final philosophical argument is consistent with the Latin sense of a fixed condition or reality.

source: 'Quaesisti proxime, Fabi frater, fugiendum necne sit in persecutione, quod nescio quid annuntiaretur.', English: 'You asked recently, brother Fabius, whether we ought to flee when persecution breaks out, prompted by some rumor I haven't quite caught.'
